knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 2.6.5
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly defines the one-sample t statistic for a Normal population with unknown σ?
knowledge_checks.body: Select the statistic, use case, and degrees of freedom.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Estimating σ with S introduces t uncertainty, and the standard error remains S/√n.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: T=(X̄-μ)/(S/√n)~t_{n-1} for a Normal sample with unknown σ.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Using S as though it were known σ in a z law or omitting √n.

choices.label: T=(X̄-μ)/(S/√n) has a t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom when sampling from a Normal population and σ is unknown.
T=(X̄-μ)/S has t_n because dividing by √n is unnecessary.
Replacing σ by S in a z statistic leaves an exact standard Normal distribution.
The t statistic is used only for comparing two sample variances.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 2.6.5
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. A Normal sample has unknown population standard deviation. Which statement gives the correct pivot for μ and correctly refuses 'The t-statistic finished the F variance-ratio LO and Chapter 3'?
knowledge_checks.body: Identify the t pivot and its boundary.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: The t pivot uses the estimated standard error and n-1 degrees of freedom. Variance ratios use F, not t.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Use (X̄-μ)/(S/√n)~t_{n-1}; refuse The t-statistic finished the F variance-ratio LO.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Using a z law with S or treating t as the variance-ratio distribution.

choices.label: (X̄-μ)/(S/√n)~t_{n-1}. This supports inference for μ, but does not by itself give the F law for comparing variances, so The t-statistic finished the F variance-ratio LO is false.
(X̄-μ)/(S/√n)~N(0,1) exactly because S and σ are interchangeable.
(X̄-μ)/S~t_{n-1} because S is already a standard error.
S₁²/S₂²~t_{n-1} because t is the standard law for variance ratios.

worked_example.title: Evaluate a one-sample t-statistic under Normal sampling
worked_example.problem_statement: A random sample of size n = 16 from a Normal population yields X̄ = 105 and sample standard deviation S = 8. Under H₀: μ = 100, compute the t-statistic and state its null degrees of freedom. Explain why replacing S by the unknown σ in a z formula is not available here.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form t = (X̄ − μ₀)/(S/√n) and name df = n − 1.

steps.label: Form the standard error using S
steps.explanation: With σ unknown, the studentised mean uses the sample sd in the denominator.

steps.label: Evaluate t and degrees of freedom
steps.explanation: Under Normal sampling and H₀, t follows Student-t with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

steps.label: Refuse z-with-S and F swallow
steps.attempt_cue: State why a z pivot with S is not the t law, and why F is a different job.
steps.explanation: Using S inside a Normal z formula pretends σ is known. The t law accounts for estimating σ. An F comparison of two sample variances is a different sampling problem from this one-sample mean pivot.
steps.calculation: z-with-S ≠ t_{15}; F is for variance ratios, not this mean pivot
steps.result: Use t_{15}, not z-with-S or F

worked_example.final_answer: t = 2.5 on 15 degrees of freedom. With σ unknown, the correct pivot is t, not a z that plugs in S, and not an F variance-ratio statistic.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Computing z = (105 − 100)/(8/4) = 2.5 and treating it as standard Normal because the arithmetic matches t, or reaching for an F statistic when the question is about a single mean.
